comments: 35 pages including supplementary material; 15 figures, 32 tables

paper_title: TESS: Query-Guided Temporal Event-Structured Frame Selection for Long-Video Understanding
paper_abstract: Temporal localization in long videos is challenging because brief, question-relevant events are dispersed among extensive redundant content. Limited visual budgets increase the risk of omitting these events or their temporal context, undermining reliable reasoning. Existing frame selection methods emphasize semantic relevance or temporal coverage, often overlooking the complementary evidence needed to locate related events and establish their temporal relationships. To address this limitation, we propose TESS, a training-free framework for query-guided temporal event-structured frame selection. TESS selects frames that jointly show the reference event and the event asked about, in the required temporal order. Leveraging frozen vision-language representations, TESS integrates soft temporal gating, role-aware budget allocation, and within-role redundancy suppression to preserve complementary event evidence. Extensive experiments across four long-video understanding benchmarks and three multimodal backbones demonstrate that TESS consistently outperforms the strongest compared baseline by 4.0-5.5 percentage points under a fixed frame budget. Further analyses reveal greater improvements on longer videos and robust performance under tighter visual budgets, while independent evidence annotations confirm enhanced event and temporal-relation coverage. These findings establish explicit temporal evidence organization as an effective training-free strategy for preserving event relationships and supporting efficient temporal reasoning over long videos. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TESS_code.

paper_title: Every Edit Its Own Budget: Per-Instruction Token Freezing for Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-Edit Image Editing
paper_abstract: Accelerating instruction-based image editing when one instruction requests several edits is challenging. Many training-free accelerators for flow-matching image editors skip tokens whose prediction has stopped changing, but decide this with a single threshold for the whole image. With several edits, such a threshold, tuned for speed, freezes small and slowly settling edits first, and requested edits disappear. We propose TIDE (Training-free Instruction-aware Drift-based Editing), which gives every instruction part its own compute budget. First, TIDE finds the region of each part in the editor's own attention by unbalanced optimal transport, without masks or external models. Second, it freezes a token once its drift is small relative to its own part and moves it along the straight path to its endpoint estimate. Third, a sparse engine computes only the remaining tokens. We prove that part-agnostic rules cannot guarantee per-part error budgets, characterize the optimal per-part threshold policy up to one tie class per part, and derive when our rule attains it. On FLUX.2 Klein, one global threshold breaks at least one edit's budget in 89% of MICE-Bench images, and TIDE drops up to 77% fewer edits at matched or higher speed (48% on MICE-Bench), a gap human raters confirm. On the many-step Klein Base, TIDE is the fastest compared method on six benchmarks (4.81-4.89x) and needs 5.3x fewer TFLOPs than vanilla, the largest saving we measure. With the same settings, it is also the fastest compared method on Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, a second model family (3.46-3.52x), and drops the fewest edits on all six benchmarks. Code will be made publicly available.

paper_title: CPU-Eval: Evaluating Large Language Models for CPU Hardware Code Generation
paper_abstract: Benchmarks such as VerilogEval have supported rapid advances in hardware description language (HDL) generation by large language models (LLMs). However, recent HDL-generation systems achieve pass rates above 90% on VerilogEval, leaving limited headroom for revealing further advances. To provide a challenging target for further progress on a practically important hardware-development task, we introduce CPU-Eval, a benchmark of 339 HDL-generation problems constructed from six CPUs. Drawn from practical CPU designs, including families fabricated in silicon, the problems span CPUs from small embedded cores to Linux-capable out-of-order cores and cover diverse CPU functions written in SystemVerilog, Chisel, and SpinalHDL. In each problem, an LLM performs the real CPU-development task of generating HDL. Across seven state-of-the-art LLMs, mean pass@1 is 45.14 percentage points lower on CPU-Eval than on VerilogEval v2 Spec-to-RTL, exposing capability differences obscured by VerilogEval's high pass rates. CPU-Eval reveals that pass@1 is lower for submodules with more source-code lines, which motivates fine-grained modular design for LLM-aided hardware generation. We also show that pass@1 is lower for CPUs written in less widely used HDLs, motivating designers to verify that an LLM is sufficiently proficient at generating code in the HDL they use before deployment.
comments: Accepted as a regular paper at the 2027 Design, Automation and Test in Europe Conference (DATE 2027). 7 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables

paper_title: Optimal Transport Meets t-SNE: Integrated Visualization without Batch Effects in OT-tSNE
paper_abstract: Visual exploration is an integral step in understanding the structure of datasets. However, systematic variation between datasets collected under different conditions, known as batch effects, can obscure shared structure and complicate their joint visualization. Existing methods often rely on cross-batch nearest-neighbor relations to integrate the batches. Yet, these local correspondences can be unreliable for challenging cross-batch geometries. We propose optimal-transport t-SNE (OT-tSNE), which replaces nearest-neighbor-based matching with globally coupled affinities derived from entropic optimal transport. Controlled synthetic experiments demonstrated that nearest-neighbor-based methods can deteriorate, while optimal-transport affinities and OT-tSNE embeddings remain robust. Across seven real single-cell datasets, we benchmarked OT-tSNE against a broad range of integration and visualization methods and found that it achieves a Pareto-efficient trade-off between batch mixing and biological conservation, and integrates batches particularly well.
comments: 35 pages, 18 figures, 5 tables. Code at https://github.com/NDR-lab/ot-tsne

paper_title: Fractal Neural Synthesis: Constant-Storage Procedural Weight Derivation via Complex Quadratic Boundary Dynamics
paper_abstract: Conventional neural networks store synaptic parameters as explicit tensors whose persistent Flash footprint scales linearly (O(W)) with parameter count, constraining resource-limited edge microcontrollers. We formulate and systematically evaluate Fractal Neural Synthesis (FNS), a procedural weight derivation architecture that replaces hidden-layer matrices with a constant 24-byte coordinate seed Theta = (c_x, c_y, ell) in F_64^3 anchored near the complex quadratic bifurcation boundary dM of f_c(z) = z^2 + c. We introduce a large-bailout (R = 256) smooth escape kernel, four zero-overhead geometric sampling apertures--Cartesian Grid, coprime 3x3 Rule-of-Thirds (Z/9Z), phi-Vogel spiral, and multi-scale Harmonic Tripod--and prove conditional Kolmogorov (K_Kolm <= 192 + c_0 bits) and Shannon entropy bounds. Across magnifications zeta in [10^0, 10^8], C^1 Fourier and lattice-noise bases collapse to post-standardization rank ~2.25 and SHA-256 PRNG exhibits avalanche discontinuity (rho ~ 0.019, 50.6% micro-step retention), whereas dM uniquely sustains both rank (~10.0) and local continuity (rho in [0.81, 0.97], 89.2% retention). Under leak-free 10-fold CV across four zero-scaler-byte non-linear benchmarks, FNS with an INT8 readout surpasses 0-hidden Linear-INT8 by +3.6 to +10.8 pp while delivering 10.7x-129x total Flash reduction (725x-2,773x hidden reduction) relative to converged Float32 MLPs (90.30% Ionosphere in 285 B; 97.22% Optical Digits in 2,598 B; 97.90% PenDigits in 2,598 B; 87.00% Satimage in 1,570 B).
comments: 14 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Reproducible code, seeds, and raw benchmark telemetry archived under Zenodo Concept DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22774934

paper_title: Can AI Design a Better nnU-Net? A Hypothesis-Driven Architecture Discovery Loop from Failures to Design Rules
paper_abstract: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.

paper_title: Improving Character Identity Consistency in Diffusion-Based Visual Story Generation through Identity Memory and Automatic Reranking
paper_abstract: Automatic visual story generation using diffusion-based models has become an increasingly important research direction in generative artificial intelligence. However, maintaining character identity consistency across consecutive frames remains an open challenge, as existing models often produce significant variations in facial traits, clothing, visual style, or anatomical proportions. This paper proposes a modular pipeline to improve character identity consistency in multi-frame visual story generation using Stable Diffusion XL alongside additional conditioning and automatic selection mechanisms. The proposed system integrates LoRA fine-tuning for character personalization, ControlNet for pose-based structural control, and IP-Adapter for visual identity transfer. Furthermore, a reranking mechanism based on Best-of-K candidate selection and persistent identity memory is introduced to automatically select the most visually consistent generated images. The work also includes integrating and extending the StoryDiffusion framework into a reproducible local workflow, along with improvements for generated frame selection. Performance evaluation uses automatic metrics such as CLIP image similarity, DINO similarity, and CLIP text-image alignment. Experimental evaluation was conducted on a custom benchmark of multiple characters and visual stories organized into difficulty levels (easy, medium, and difficult). Both progressive variants of the proposed pipeline and extended versions of StoryDiffusion were evaluated, including SDXL baseline, Best-of-K, Identity Memory, and the Full Pipeline. Results show that reranking, identity memory, and visual conditioning reduce identity drift across frames and improve the overall coherence and stability of generated visual stories.
comments: 12 pages, 9 figures. Project repository available at: https://github.com/MerryWex/character-consistency-visual-storytelling

paper_title: Functional Divergence of Upper- and Lower-Body Fat Distribution and Differences in Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease Risk and Outcomes: A Narrative Review
paper_abstract: Traditional obesity risk assessment centers on body mass index (BMI); however, marked differences in cardiovascular and cerebrovascular outcomes despite comparable total adiposity suggest that the regional attributes of adipose tissue have independent explanatory value. Consistent evidence from cohort studies and Mendelian randomization (MR) shows that upper-body (abdominal/truncal) fat is positively associated with cardiovascular and cerebrovascular risk, whereas lower-body (gluteofemoral/leg) fat is independently associated with reduced risk at the adipose depot volume level. In a South Indian dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) study, each 1-SD increase in android fat was associated with an odds ratio (OR) for type 2 diabetes of 6.59 (95% CI, 3.17–13.70) in men, whereas the OR for leg fat was 0.42 (95% CI, 0.24–0.74). A dose-response meta-analysis showed that each 10-cm increase in hip circumference was associated with a 10% lower risk of all-cause mortality (hazard ratio (HR), 0.90; 95% CI, 0.81–0.99); after adjustment for BMI and waist circumference, the association strengthened to an HR of 0.78 (95% CI, 0.66–0.90). Data from the UK Biobank showed that, after adjustment for BMI and waist circumference, each 1-SD increase in hip circumference was associated with a 5% lower risk of coronary heart disease (HR, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.93–0.97). A cross-cohort reclassification analysis showed that among individuals with a "normal-weight" BMI, 5% had an elevated waist circumference and 18% had an elevated waist-to-hip ratio; most of these individuals, who were not identified by BMI-based classification, had a 15%–50% increased risk of cardiovascular outcomes. A Chinese population cohort showed that dynamic changes in the weight-adjusted waist index were independently associated with cardiovascular and cerebrovascular mortality, with the group showing the largest increase having a 1.52-fold higher risk than the lowest group. Upper-body fat risk exhibited a dose-dependent pattern: a high visceral adiposity index was associated with a 55% increased risk of cardiovascular disease (risk ratio (RR), 1.55; 95% CI, 1.36–1.76). The causal signal for visceral adipose tissue (VAT) is highly sensitive to exposure definition and inferential framework. Within an MR framework using MRI-measured VAT volume and BMI adjustment, VAT had no robust effect on atherosclerotic outcomes. In contrast, observational associations of BMI-adjusted MRI-defined VAT showed a positive signal. An MR study across multiple vascular beds used MRI-derived fat depots as exposure measures. After BMI adjustment, each 1-SD increase in gluteofemoral adipose tissue (GFAT) volume was associated with 17%, 24%, and 28% lower risks of myocardial infarction, large-artery atherosclerotic stroke, and peripheral artery disease, respectively. These effects attenuated but remained significant after adjustment for lipids. In contrast, causal estimates for waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) and hip circumference were not robust in sensitivity analyses. Sex-specific MR showed that the causal association between WHR and coronary heart disease was significant in women (OR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.06–1.26) but not in men. At the mechanistic level, paired chromatin landscape analysis of subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) and omental visceral adipose tissue (OVAT) showed that OVAT-specific differentially accessible regions were approximately twice as numerous as those in SAT and were enriched at promoters of cardiomyopathy-related genes. AI-driven large-scale clinical phenotyping in 101,243 patients showed that individuals positive for brown adipose tissue (BAT) had a lower prevalence of cardiovascular and psychiatric diseases. Higher BAT activity was associated with lower odds of cardiometabolic disease, and angiotensin receptor blocker use was positively associated with BAT, suggesting that BAT has preliminary druggable-target signals, although causal and hard-endpoint evidence is not yet established. A retrospective cohort of 13,530 patients undergoing PET/CT further showed that BAT positivity was independently associated with a lower incidence of cardiovascular events (P=0.018). Perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) and epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) influence arterial stiffness, ventricular remodeling, and arrhythmias through paracrine pathways adjacent to target organs. EAT volume was independently associated with new-onset atrial fibrillation (HR per 1-SD increase, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.05–1.58; still significant after adjustment for BMI and left atrial volume). The CT-accessible Fat Attenuation Index has translated the inflammatory phenotype of PVAT into a clinically deployable prognostic tool; pericoronary adipose tissue (PCAT) attenuation was significantly associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) risk (HR, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.38–1.81) and all-cause mortality (HR, 1.77), but this effect size was highly sensitive to analytical strategy. Radiomic quantification of EAT volume and the PVAT inflammatory phenotype jointly support the feasibility of opportunistic risk stratification. At the intervention level, several lines of evidence jointly support "distribution improvement" as an independent dimension for evaluating interventions beyond weight loss alone. These include CENTRAL/DIRECT-PLUS, the primary and mediation analyses of SELECT, comparisons of VAT reduction across different intervention pathways, the SUMMIT CMR substudy, the DAPA-EAT trial, and evidence on dapagliflozin and EAT. Heart failure outcomes exhibit heterogeneity by ejection fraction phenotype. A prospective cohort of 428,000 participants in the UK Biobank showed that heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) was independently associated with all adiposity measures (VAT: HR, 1.23), whereas heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) was not independently associated with adiposity measures. EAT was consistently associated with harm in HFpEF/heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) but showed a paradoxical association in HFrEF. Among patients with HFpEF, 91% had an elevated waist circumference and 85% had elevated VAT, but only 38% met the BMI criterion for obesity. The PARAGON-HF trial further showed that the prevalence of central obesity (waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) ≥0.5) in HFpEF was as high as 96%, whereas BMI-defined obesity was present in only 49%. In diabetic HFrEF, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR)-defined sarcopenic obesity was independently associated with approximately a 3-fold risk of adverse outcomes (HR, 3.03; 95% CI, 1.39–6.63). Three-dimensional deep learning segmentation of whole-body MRI has enabled direct quantification of GFAT and provided incremental discrimination of ΔAUC 0.01–0.02 beyond models already containing BMI and WHR. A sarcopenic obesity index derived from routine CMR (body weight/pectoralis major mass) in 55,768 UK Biobank CMR scans showed that each 1-SD increase was associated with a 31% higher risk of incident heart failure, a 51% higher risk of cardiovascular death, and a 37% higher risk of all-cause death. This index provides a scalable operational tool for characterizing the "fat–muscle configuration." AI-derived MRI body composition analysis further showed that, after full adjustment for BMI and waist circumference, only VAT proportion and skeletal muscle fat fraction independently provided incremental prognostic information for MACE. This suggests that opportunistic radiomic quantification is extending beyond the boundaries of circumference-based proxies. Critical benchmarking of novel body shape indices suggests that BMI combined with WHR captures nearly all body shape information relevant to cardiometabolic disease; novel indices have incremental value but are not yet sufficient to support widespread replacement of BMI + WHR. The Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) cohort showed that WHR significantly modifies the cardiovascular risk associated with lipoprotein(a) (Lp[a]): individuals with Lp(a) ≥50 mg/dL and WHR ≥90th percentile had the highest atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) incidence (35.7/1,000 person-years). The American Diabetes Association (ADA) 2026 standards and the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome guideline have incorporated distribution indicators such as waist circumference into risk stratification; the Expert Consensus on the Management of Obesity in the Elderly (2026 Edition) further provides diagnostic cutoffs for waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio in Chinese older adults. This narrative review synthesizes the above evidence, using "functional divergence" as the organizing thread.

paper_title: Physics-Only, Data-Driven and Physics-Informed Hybrid Capacity Prognostics for Li-Ion Cells: A Leave-One-Battery-Out Evaluation on NASA PCoE Data and Implications for Rail Duty Cycles
paper_abstract: Physics-informed hybrid models are often reported as better than purely physical or purely data-driven prognostics, usually on same-cell train/test splits. We test this under a leave-one-battery-out (LOBO) protocol on four NASA PCoE Li-ion cells (B0005, B0006, B0007, B0018), comparing (i) a power-law model fitted to the first 30% of each cell’s life and extrapolated, (ii) a Gaussian process regression (GPR) trained on the other three cells, and (iii) a hybrid that adds a pooled GPR residual correction to the power-law fit. The data-driven model gave the lowest mean held-out RMSE (118.4 mAh), followed by the hybrid (173.0 mAh) and the physics-only model (321.0 mAh). The hybrid beat the data-driven model on one cell (B0018: 87.4 vs. 190.9 mAh) but was worse on the other three, most strongly on B0006 (361.1 vs. 94.7 mAh), where the physics-only extrapolation was the best of the three (51.7 mAh). With four cells, none of these differences can be tested statistically, and the data-driven and hybrid models use cycle-concurrent health indicators, so they perform health estimation rather than forecasting. A pooled residual correction therefore cannot be assumed to help. We outline what a test on non-stationary rail duty cycles would require.

paper_title: How Professional Background Influences the Evaluation of Human- and AI-Generated Posters
paper_abstract: Ten expert judges independently evaluated 84 environmental advocacy posters using the Consensual Assessment Technique, and full-panel inter-rater reliability was very low: Krippendorff's alpha was .10 for Technical Execution, .07 for Conceptual Originality, and .07 for Emotional Resonance, with bootstrapped confidence intervals far below the .667 floor Krippendorff (2019) treated as minimally acceptable. The posters had been produced by 28 design students as coursework under three conditions varying whether the idea, the execution, or both came from generative AI; because the instrument failed, condition comparisons could not be meaningfully carried out. The shortfall was not evenly distributed. Splitting the panel by professional background revealed genuine, if modest, agreement among the five industry judges (α = .23 to .36, still short of the .667 floor) alongside near-total disagreement among the five academic judges (α near zero), indicating that reliability depended on panel composition rather than being impossible in principle. Within-poster standard deviations averaged around 1.3 points on a five-point scale, showing that judges applied systematically different standards. This pattern fit accounts treating aesthetic judgment as intersubjective, grounded in communities of shared practice, rather than purely subjective. These findings caution against summative judgments from mixed professional panels and support process-oriented, multi-perspective evaluation.

paper_title: From Retrieval to Answerability: Versioned Evidence, Permission-Bound Search, and Institutional Control in Cloud Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is often described as a means of reducing unsupported answers by connecting a language model to an external collection of documents. In regulated cloud environments, however, a cited answer may still rely on an outdated document, an unauthorised passage, or an unreviewable sequence of processing decisions. This article develops an evidence-and-authority model of RAG trustworthiness. It uses a bounded, critical documentary synthesis of recent literature on cloud RAG and cyber-threat intelligence, together with relevant standards and closely related 2026 scholarship. The synthesis is interpretive rather than a systematic review or an empirical performance study. It identifies three necessary but non-substitutable functions: versioned provenance, permission-bound information flow, and actionable governance. The contribution is a set of testable control invariants, a query-level evidence record, an intervention ladder, and an evaluation protocol that distinguishes correct retrieval from supported answers, access control from information-flow protection, and audit completeness from effective accountability. Two hypothetical scenarios demonstrate how the architecture would handle policy revision and malicious semantic-cache reuse. The model also makes its limits explicit: it does not establish legal compliance, provide measured performance gains, or replace community authority over knowledge. Trustworthy RAG is proposed as a continuing organisational capacity to show what knowledge was used, why its use was permitted, and how an affected person can challenge the outcome.

paper_title: Terpene-Based Polymer Nanocomposites Through Green Chemistry: Incorporation of Algerian Maghnite-CTA⁺ and Evaluation of Antibacterial Performance
paper_abstract: This study explores a sustainable approach to the development of terpene-based copoly-mers and nanocomposites using β-pinene and β-myrcene as renewable starting materials and a natural nanoclay (Mag-CTA+) as a reinforcing agent. The β-pinene/β-myrcene co-polymer (βp-co-βmy) was synthesized through cationic copolymerization using AlCl₃ as a Lewis acid catalyst. Its chemical structure and thermal behavior were investigated by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), proton and carbon nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H-NMR and 13C-NMR), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Nano-composites containing 2, 5, 8, and 10% by weight of Mag-CTA+, were then prepared by solution blending assisted by ultrasonic irradiation to improve filler dispersion within the polymer matrix. The resulting materials were characterized using FT-IR, X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to examine their structural and morphological features. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) showed that nanoclay incorporation improved the thermal stability of the copoly-mer. Microscopic observations further revealed that the dispersion of the clay depended on its loading. At 2 wt%, the Mag-CTA+ was predominantly exfoliated within the polymer matrix, whereas higher contents (5–10 wt%) led to increasingly intercalated structures and partial aggregation. The antibacterial activity of the prepared terpene-based copolymer and its nanocomposites was evaluated against selected bacterial strains. The results pro-vide insight into the potential of incorporating natural nanoclay into terpene-based poly-mer matrices to influence their antibacterial performance. The combination of renewable terpene-derived polymers and nanoclay represents a promising approach for developing functional materials with improved thermal stability and potential antibacterial proper-ties. These materials may be of interest for future applications in active food packaging and biomedical materials, although further investigations are required to clarify their an-tibacterial mechanisms and assess their safety and effectiveness under applica-tion-relevant conditions.

paper_title: Variant-Aware CRISPR Diagnostics Under Pathogen Evolution: From Computational Design to Clinical Translation and Adaptive Updating
paper_abstract: CRISPR-based diagnostics (CRISPR-Dx) have emerged as programmable platforms for rapid nucleic acid detection, but their reliable translation is challenged by continuous pathogen genomic evolution. Sequence variation can alter target conservation, primer compatibility, guide activity, and variant discrimination, making reference-based design increasingly inadequate. This review examines CRISPR-Dx as a computationally informed, multistage design problem in which pathogen diversity, target selection, primer-guide compatibility, functional prediction, evolutionary objectives, and downstream diagnostic constraints are interconnected. It synthesizes approaches spanning whole-genome and population-aware target discovery, integrated primer-guide design, machine-learning-based guide prediction, computational benchmarking, variant-resilient and discriminatory targeting, guide engineering, and model-directed sequence generation. Particular emphasis is placed on separating computational evidence from experimental, analytical, clinical, and deployment evidence, because improvements in upstream prediction do not necessarily translate proportionally into diagnostic performance. Resilience, which seeks sustained detection across evolving pathogen populations, is distinguished from discrimination, which exploits defined sequence differences for variant identification. Building on these observations, an adaptive CRISPR-Dx framework is proposed that links surveillance, design, testing, deployment, and updating. The major unresolved challenge is establishing this cycle prospectively, with explicit validation thresholds, uncertainty management, and regulatory control, under real-world pathogen evolution.

paper_title: Computational Verification and Numerical Precision of Research Foundation Analyzer v6.0 Relative to Commercial Statistical Packages
paper_abstract: This study evaluates the computational benchmarking and numerical reliability of Research Foundation Analyzer v6.0 against local Python scripting engines (Statsmodels, SciPy, Scikit-learn) and industry-standard statistical software, including SAS Studio Enterprise Edition, GraphPad Prism (version 10.0), and Microsoft Excel. Engineered to address prohibitive licensing costs and data security risks associated with cloud computation, the application executes a Python backend (v3.11.3) via a local Client-Side WebAssembly/Pyodide architecture, ensuring zero remote data transmission and complete user data sovereignty. Algorithmic precision was systematically verified across seven core empirical research scenarios: One-Way ANOVA under Completely Randomized Design (CRD), One-Way ANOVA under Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD), Two-Way Factorial ANOVA (3×3), Sensory Evaluation under RCBD, multivariate Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Bivariate Pearson Correlation, and 3D Multiple Linear Regression. Across all evaluated parameters—including sum of squares, degrees of freedom, mean squares, F-values, exact probability values (p-values), automated Tukey's HSD letter designations, PCA eigenvalues, component loadings, Pearson coefficients (r), and regression estimators (R², RMSE)—Research Foundation Analyzer v6.0 achieved absolute numerical parity (Δ = 0, representing 100% computational identity) against all reference suites. Partitioning of experimental error, isolation of blocking variance (RCBD, p = 0.0025), and automated post-hoc letterings matched SAS (PROC GLM) and Python scripts with zero divergence. Furthermore, the platform integrates workflow automation through structured Grid Matrix inputs, high-resolution vector graphics (heatmaps, biplots, response surfaces), and instantaneous formatted Microsoft Word (.docx) export. These findings confirm that running scientific Python routines inside a local WebAssembly environment maintains full 64-bit IEEE 754 precision without computational drift, establishing Research Foundation Analyzer v6.0 as an institutional-grade, accessible, and privacy-preserving computational tool for higher education, graduate research, and peer-reviewed scientific publishing.

paper_title: Language Models Steer on Injected Uncertainty Tokens, but Fail to Self-Monitor In Situ
paper_abstract: Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control.   On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.

paper_title: Self-Supervised Dataset Distillation via Mutual Information Maximization
paper_abstract: Dataset distillation (DD) aims to compress a large dataset into a small synthetic one that remains effective for training neural networks. Despite its success in supervised learning, DD remains underexplored in self-supervised learning (SSL), where distilled data must preserve the information needed to learn representations that remain consistent across augmentations. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mutual Information Prototype Alignment (MIPA), an efficient SSL dataset distillation approach that optimizes synthetic images to preserve augmentation-invariant information. Specifically, MIPA treats synthetic images as learnable prototypes and uses a frozen encoder to assign real samples to them based on feature similarity. A synthetic dataset that preserves such augmentation invariance should yield stable prototype assignments across multiple augmented views of the same real image. MIPA encourages this by maximizing mutual information between cross-view assignments while avoiding trivial solutions in which all real samples are assigned to only a few synthetic prototypes. Evaluations on image classification benchmarks show that synthetic data generated by MIPA yield higher-quality representations than existing distillation approaches while reducing time and storage demands during distillation.

paper_title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning
paper_abstract: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.

paper_title: WorldLatent: A Unified 4D Latent Space for World Perception and Generation
paper_abstract: Generative Pre-Training (GPT) represents a profound milestone in natural language processing, serving as the foundation for most of today's state-of-the-art large language models. By casting diverse understanding and generation problems into a shared token representation, GPT enables a single architecture and unified optimization loop to master heterogeneous tasks across massive corpora, giving rise to powerful foundation models for natural language. In contrast, 4D spatiotemporal vision lacks a common representational protocol: perception (such as depth and camera estimation) and generation are either handled by separate one-way pipelines or bolted together from unaligned single-modality spaces. In this work, we introduce WorldLatent, a framework that formulates a unified 4D latent space as a common protocol for both world perception and generation. Rather than relying on fragmented, task-specific models or stacked single-modality representations, our framework proposes a multimodal VAE architecture that compresses and fuses complex 4D visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into a single structured latent representation. Within this formulation, perception and generation operate as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space, enabling one generative model to learn both capabilities simultaneously within a single training loop. Experiments across representative 4D benchmarks verify that our fused latent protocol achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent 4D generation, and controllable editing from a single model. By demonstrating that diverse 4D tasks can be seamlessly unified under a shared representational protocol, our work provides a scalable foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.

paper_title: Matching Under Metric Privacy
paper_abstract: We study how to represent and randomize points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space to obtain accurate bipartite matchings under metric privacy. Given $n$ private and $n$ public points, we analyze local mechanisms that randomize each private point or its distances to the public points. Using the public points' affine span, we construct a smaller representation that preserves all matching costs. When a trusted server receives the private points, we establish privacy and utility guarantees for Gumbel matching, which randomizes edge costs and releases only the assignment. Through upper bounds and worst-case constructions, we establish the tight rate $Θ\!\left(n\min\{d,\log n\}/\varepsilon\right)$ for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum. Benchmark experiments support $d\approx\log n$ as a practical guide to the transition between directly randomizing point coordinates and using Gumbel matching. Extensions to squared Euclidean costs enable private nonparametric two-sample hypothesis testing. These results show how the application's trust model guides representation and dimension choices for better utility: under local privacy, low-dimensional point representations reduce excess cost, while under central privacy, distance representations achieve the optimal rate even in high dimension.

paper_title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents
paper_abstract: Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. Human practitioners, by contrast, cope with insufficient tools by fashioning new ones from familiar parts and reusing them across tasks. Inspired by this, we propose ToolSmith, an automatic tool-generation framework that grows and reuses modules on top of a lean base tool library. We evaluate ToolSmith on three in-domain multimodal search benchmarks and ten out-of-domain benchmarks under a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol. ToolSmith consistently improves over the base library across deployed agents of varying scales, with larger backbones reaping greater gains, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Our code and data are available at https://threesr.github.io/toolsmith/.

paper_title: Attention Latent Feedback
paper_abstract: During autoregressive decoding, the deeper representations of the previous token have already been computed, yet shallow layers at the current token cannot read them directly because standard self-attention connects positions only at the same depth. We introduce Attention Latent Feedback (ALF), an architecture that allows every sublayer to attend to the outputs of the deeper layers at the previous position. Training unrolls this cross-position recurrence into two parallel passes, whereas decoding remains single-pass using cached previous-token states. Across mixture-of-experts models with up to 4.0B parameters, ALF lowers held-out loss by 0.022-0.024 nats over the standard residual with about 1.1% decoding FLOP overhead, and consistently outperforms prior final-state feedback across all three scales on both standard and attention residual backbones. On MoE-1.6B, ALF matches a $1.38\times$ larger baseline token budget, and on MoE-4.0B it lifts average accuracy across seventeen downstream benchmarks from 45.1% to 47.0%. Analysis further reveals that intermediate and nearby deeper layers drive most of this benefit, allowing a fixed nearest-window variant to retain 89%-94% of the gain at linear read cost while learned attention widens its margin with scale.

paper_title: LiveLoRA: Exact KV Cache Migration Across LoRA Updates for LLM Agents
paper_abstract: Updating an LLM adapter should not require replaying the full interaction history of every active session. Yet reusing key-value (KV) cache entries computed under an earlier version mixes model versions, while full-history re-prefill becomes increasingly costly as histories and session fleets grow. We introduce LiveLora, a model-runtime co-design for exact final-block KV cache migration. Frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections preserve each token's base projections and low-rank coordinates across adapter versions. The runtime reconstructs candidate K/V, reevaluates the latest token through the final block, and commits the adapter, cache, and next-token logits together. We prove continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under the stated model assumptions. On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, median paired publication speedups over full-history re-prefill average $68.98\times$ across five runs for 32 active sessions with 8K tokens each. Serving benchmarks show approximately 4.8% decoding overhead relative to native cached decoding. Compared with retained-boundary replay, compact retention gives a $3.42\times$ reduction in additional session storage at 8K, with similar measured publication-plus-decoding cost. LiveLora allows persistent LLM agents to adopt new adapter versions without replaying their full interaction histories.
comments: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop AgenticOS: Co-designing Systems and ML Foundations of an OS Layer for Agentic AI

paper_title: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals
paper_abstract: Looped Transformers iterate a shared block of layers to increase computation without adding parameters, offering stronger performance and test-time scaling. However, this power has so far required training from scratch and yielded only modest gains for LLMs. Finetuning existing models into loops is far cheaper, yet also brings only marginal gains over SFT. We propose LoopRes, an effective, scalable, and simple approach that turns loops into significant and consistent gains for pretrained LLMs. Building on Attention Residuals, LoopRes lets each looped layer attend directly to the outputs of earlier loops. Since these outputs are iterates of the same layers and become harder to tell apart, we give each a trainable loop-aware key that encodes its structural identity. Attending to all earlier loops also lets layers skip intermediate ones, so we restrict each layer to a residual window of the latest W loops, forcing every loop to build incrementally on recent ones. Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains: at 2x compute, it improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the state-of-the-art baseline. The gains hold on larger models up to 30B and across all three families. More importantly, from 1.7B to 8B, LoopRes scales more steeply than SFT as compute grows, reaching a higher ceiling while needing less compute on long outputs. These results establish LoopRes as an effective looping approach, delivering both better performance and better test-time scaling.

paper_title: UMAMI: A Multimodal Benchmark Dataset for Evidence-Grounded Dietary Decisions
paper_abstract: Dietary decisions require identifying a food's nutrient content and considering individual dietary needs, but recognizing food from an image alone does not provide this information. Visually similar foods can have different nutrient profiles, so selecting the wrong food record can lead to incorrect decisions even when nutrient rules are applied correctly. Furthermore, satisfying nutrient constraints does not necessarily establish a food's relevance to a person's intake. Evaluating these challenges together requires connecting food images, nutrient records, and individual intake histories. To support this evaluation, we introduce UMAMI (Unified Multimodal Assessment of Meals and Intake), a multimodal dataset and benchmark linking independently collected food images with nutrient profiles and respondent health and intake records. Using this dataset, we construct three diagnostic tasks covering visual nutrient question answering, personalized food recommendation, and condition-aware food substitution. Paired instances and input controls examine how visual identity and respondent context affect decisions. Our experiments identify errors in both food-record selection and nutrient-rule application, while showing that higher rule compliance does not necessarily improve alignment with subsequent recorded intake. These findings highlight the need to evaluate how multimodal systems select and use structured evidence for dietary decisions. The dataset, code, and dashboard are available at https://umami-benchmark.github.io.
comments: 40 pages, 15 figures, 16 tables. Dataset, code, and dashboard: https://umami-benchmark.github.io

paper_title: From Local Errors to System Failures: Modeling and Benchmarking Error Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
paper_abstract: In multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs), errors can propagate through intermediate messages and compromise final answers. However, outcome-based evaluation obscures how agents amplify, attenuate, or correct these errors. We propose Response-Aware Error Propagation among Agents (REPA), a structural model that connects measured local responses to system-level error propagation. REPA separately estimates input assembly and agent processing across multiple error channels, while theoretical analysis relates local modeling errors to endpoint prediction error. Experiments span three Qwen base models, six MAS workflows, and ten knowledge and reasoning settings in ErrPropBench-10. REPA achieves a mean condition-level Spearman correlation of 0.84 across base models, compared with 0.47 for direct regression. Controlled experiments also demonstrate its utility for targeted recovery. REPA-guided retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves accuracy over no retrieval by an average of 19 percentage points with 16% additional tokens. By linking local agent behavior to system susceptibility, REPA provides an interpretable foundation for studying error propagation and developing targeted optimization in MAS.

paper_title: Boltz-Flow: Generating High-Quality Robot Action from Boltzmann Machine
paper_abstract: Flow-matching policies integrate a velocity field from a fixed, observation-independent Gaussian source. However, since the source is unimodal and identical across all tasks, the limited representational capacity of Gaussian distributions constrains how far a policy can scale with growing task diversity. Moreover, the source factorizes over time steps and control dimensions, discarding the coordination that manipulation requires. We introduce Boltz-Flow, which replaces Gaussian initialization with a more powerful, observation- and instruction-conditioned Boltzmann source while leaving the base VLA unchanged. Boltz-Flow parameterizes this source with a conditional Boltzmann machine that assigns an energy value to each binary source state. A listwise objective, supervised entirely by offline demonstrations, aligns this energy with the quality of actions produced after frozen flow integration. At inference, the energy defines an Ising instance whose solution is decoded into continuous noise before a single standard integration. We use a physical coherent Ising machine during training. Experiments show that Boltz-Flow improves $π_{0.5}$ across three benchmarks, outperforming the compared strong policy baselines and competing noise optimization methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 and ranking second only to LEAP on LIBERO-Plus. Additional experiments show gains under noise-adapted fine-tuning, with action-to-action warm starts, and on the SmolVLA backbone.

paper_title: Déjà VAE: When Do Autoencoder Traces Reveal Generated Images?
paper_abstract: A latent diffusion model's output has already passed through its autoencoder, so a second round trip changes it very little. This "déjà vu" underlies reconstruction-based detectors of generated images; we analyse when it reveals a generated image and when it does not. Read by a frozen vision foundation model without training, the trace is strongest in intermediate layers, and, unlike pixel-level reconstruction error, it treats blur as a sign of a real image. It belongs to the generator's exact decoder: on Synthbuster, the exact decoders of Stable Diffusion 1.3, 1.4, 2 and XL are the strongest of eight autoencoders and catch 94-100% of their generators' images at a 5% false-alarm rate (SDXL's version identified post hoc), while near-identical versions catch 7-42%. A detector trained only on real photographs and their autoencoder copies matches one trained on 162k generated images on GenImage (+2.3 points, 95% CI [0.9, 3.7]) and complements it in fusion, but one resize with JPEG re-save, or a mild blur, costs it 19-27 points. Two lessons concern benchmarks. The in-the-wild benchmark Chameleon can be solved from image width alone. And on Synthbuster, how the real photographs are matched to the generated images' size decides whether our detector leads or trails (+4.4 or -9.7 points): the matching protocol alone can reverse a detector comparison. Code and per-image scores: https://github.com/iamsaugatpandey/deja-vae
comments: 29 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Code and per-image scores: https://github.com/iamsaugatpandey/deja-vae

paper_title: ComputeWise: Measuring and Fixing GPU Waste by AI Research Agents
paper_abstract: AI agents are given GPUs to do AI research on their own. Do they use those GPUs well? A busy GPU does not tell us, because it can be busy with work the answer did not need. This matters, because the tokens the agent spends cost almost nothing next to the GPUs its experiments run on, so using those GPUs better has a huge impact. So we built ComputeWise, an open benchmark of research tasks on which this waste can be measured and reduced. For it we developed our own simulated GPU, which replays recorded runs to the agent's code. With no real GPU needed, we ran hundreds of experiments, far more than would be reasonable on real GPUs. With no help, the agents put only 52% of their GPU time into work the answer needed. Another 22% went to work it did not need, and 26% sat idle. Asking the agent to finish the work faster, telling it to keep every GPU busy, or giving it a job scheduler does not fix this. So we built an open-source harness, part prompting and part deterministic code. Across five models, it removed over 80% of the extra time to the answer.
comments: 11 pages, 5 figures. Preliminary version; a revised version is in preparation. Code: https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/computewise. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Salesforce/computewise

paper_title: WildAnySplat: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting in the Wild
paper_abstract: We present WildAnySplat, a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that enables robust novel-view synthesis from in-the-wild multi-view images. Unlike controlled captures, real-world images often contain multi-view inconsistencies caused by transient occluders, illumination changes, and camera ISP, which degrade the quality of existing feed-forward reconstruction methods.   To address this challenge, we introduce a student-teacher framework that learns transient-robust and appearance-consistent 3D representations. A teacher network operates on clean images, while a student processes the corresponding in-the-wild inputs. The teacher provides clean supervision to guide the student toward a consistent canonical representation. Since paired clean and in-the-wild data are scarce, we use a hybrid data strategy, combining real paired captures, synthetic augmentations, and pseudo-clean labels generated from optimization-based reconstructions, bridging the domain gap between synthetic and real-world data.   We adopt a transformer architecture with dedicated DPT heads for camera pose, depth, and Gaussian prediction. We additionally predict per-view transient masks to reweight photometric supervision and suppress unreliable Gaussians. To account for cross-view appearance variation, we incorporate a bilateral grid module that models per-image color transformations and enables recovery of a canonical radiance representation.   Experiments on challenging in-the-wild benchmarks show that WildAnySplat improves robustness to transient occlusions and appearance variation while retaining the fast inference of feed-forward Gaussian Splatting.
comments: Accepted to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 (Conference Papers). Project page: https://wildanysplat.github.io/ ; Supplementary material: https://wildanysplat.github.io/wildanysplat_supp.pdf

paper_title: OmniV-Bench: Can MLLMs Comprehend Immersive Spatio-temporal Scenes?
paper_abstract: Omnidirectional videos (ODVs) capture dynamic environments with a full $360^\circ$ field of view, providing rich spatial context and temporal dynamics for applications such as virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and embodied intelligence. Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made great progress in spatial and temporal understanding, yet their ability to comprehend the immersive 360 spatio-temporal information conveyed by ODVs remains largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we first introduce OmniV-Bench, a Benchmark designed to comprehensively evaluate the capabilities of MLLMs on spatio-temporal Omnidirectional Video understanding. OmniV-Bench contains 4,123 high-quality ODVs collected from diverse scenes, along with 8,923 human-annotated question-answer pairs spanning 11 fine-grained tasks across three categories, i.e., general, spatial, and spatio-temporal understanding. Extensive benchmark experiments reveal that the spatio-temporal complexity of ODVs poses significant challenges for current MLLMs. To address these limitations, we further propose OmniV-Harness, an agentic harness that enhances ODV understanding through viewpoint-guided evidence initialization and task-relevant evidence acquisition with adaptive tool use. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that OmniV-Harness consistently improves immersive spatio-temporal reasoning ability of MLLMs. Both OmniV-Bench and OmniV-Harness will be released upon publication.

paper_title: Lorentz symmetry in self-supervised representation learning
paper_abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) and explicit physical inductive biases have driven major advances in jet tagging, yet they are typically pursued along separate tracks. In this work, we unify both paradigms by integrating the Lorentz-equivariant Geometric Algebra Transformer slim (L-GATr-slim) architecture with the LeJEPA framework for representation learning. Pre-training on 100 million jets from the JetClass dataset, we optimize towards a latent space, which is invariant across physics-motivated jet augmentations. We demonstrate that enforcing Lorentz symmetry in the latent space is critical for representation quality and that this can be achieved either architecturally or learned via kinematic augmentations. With a standard non-invariant Transformer backbone, LeJEPA outperforms established autoregressive, masked particle modelling, and self-distillation baselines in linear- and MLP-probe accuracy, with L-GATr-slim providing further complementary gains. Across downstream benchmarks, our pre-trained models consistently outperform baselines trained from scratch or through different pre-training objectives.

paper_title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching
paper_abstract: Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. However, we reveal that existing methods essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR), regressing the \emph{trainable policy} velocity onto rollouts from a \emph{behavior distribution}. Unbiased baseline subtraction implicitly assumes that the policy velocity equals the behavior marginal velocity---an idealized assumption violated under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency. This \emph{behavior--policy mismatch} breaks baseline invariance and injects \emph{baseline-induced gradient drift}, destabilizing training. To resolve this issue, we propose \textbf{I}nstantaneous \textbf{T}rajectory \textbf{D}istribution \textbf{M}atching (\textbf{iTDM}), taking the infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching toward a time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Tracking this velocity with an online auxiliary denoiser guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, effectively suppressing baseline drift across both online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment show that iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance. Notably, on the challenging GenEval2 benchmark, iTDM converges nearly $3\times$ faster than competing methods while scaling smoothly to $0.87$ without collapse. Code is available at https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM

paper_title: MedUIGym: Evaluating and Training GUI Agents for Clinical Workflows
paper_abstract: Automating clinical workflows requires vision-language agents that can navigate dense graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in electronic health records (EHRs) and execute precise actions, yet many medical agents still rely on text or structured tool calls. In this work, we introduce MedUIGym, a scalable interactive environment comprising 15,739 tasks from 17 benchmark sources across six clinical task families for training and evaluating clinical GUI agents. In MedUIGym, agents perceive EHR states from screenshots and execute mouse-and-keyboard actions, as well as a paired native-tool interface over identical clinical data. The environment verifies both final answers and required clinical actions, and supports parallel trajectory collection for training. Benchmarking twelve vision-language models shows that current agents struggle across diverse clinical workflows, and simply increasing reasoning effort fails to yield consistent gains. Furthermore, MedUIGym supports offline learning from GUI trajectories and online reinforcement learning from task rewards. After training, both Qwen3.5 models perform better on in-domain clinical tasks and generalize to tasks from external sources. By unifying tasks from existing benchmarks, dual-interface evaluation, and GUI trajectory collection, MedUIGym provides a testbed for studying how vision-language agents complete clinical tasks through the EHR's graphical interface. Our project page is available at https://github.com/yitong-qiao/MedUIGym.

paper_title: Prediction-Powered Regression via Calibration: Beyond the Supervised Minimax Benchmark
paper_abstract: We study nonparametric regression with limited labeled data and abundant observations carrying potentially inaccurate pseudo-labels. Our proposed method, weighted prediction-powered regression via calibration (wPPRC), first calibrates pseudo-labels using labeled data, then fits a predictor by weighted regression using observed and calibrated responses. Over Hölder classes, we derive nonasymptotic excess-risk bounds for clipped ReLU estimators and establish a minimax lower bound for the corresponding regression problem. Under suitable conditions, the upper and lower bounds match up to logarithmic factors. Moreover, wPPRC can achieve a worst-case risk of smaller order than the minimax risks under four baseline observation structures on the same joint distribution class, demonstrating the value of additional pseudo-labels. We also construct a validation-selected (VS) estimator using an independent labeled validation sample to choose the weight. The VS estimator satisfies an expected-risk oracle inequality and preserves the improvement over the baseline minimax risks with the same total labeled-data budget. Simulations and an application to predicting homeless counts illustrate the gains of the proposed estimators.

paper_title: Self-Evolving Evaluation Environments for Computer-Use Agents
paper_abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are rapidly improving, yet their evaluation remains largely static. Existing benchmarks provide a strong foundation, but fixed difficulty ceilings, limited feature coverage, and coarse aggregate scores progressively weaken their discriminative and diagnostic value. We introduce CUA-SEE, a closed-loop evaluation environment that co-evolves tasks and executable verifiers from rollout evidence. It disentangles three objectives: benchmark evolution expands evaluation scope through cohort-calibrated difficulty and coverage growth; diagnostic evolution increases resolution through agent-conditional capability-boundary probes; and verifier evolution improves precision by translating changing requirements into state-grounded checkpoints with adversarial validation. Across multiple agents, applications, and rounds, CUA-SEE generates challenging, measurable tasks while preserving process-level evidence. Our results position adaptive evaluation as a scalable counterpart to self-evolving agents, continuously tracking what agents can do, where their boundaries lie, and how reliably progress is measured.

paper_title: SayDo: Benchmarking the Safety of Frontier Models from Chat to Closed-Loop Robot Control
paper_abstract: Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level robot controllers, yet their safety is evaluated almost entirely in text. We introduce SayDo, a benchmark that assesses the propensity of frontier models to cause harm in embodied contexts. SayDo comprises eleven laboratory and household tasks that pair a benign instruction with a hazard latent in the scene. Tasks are implemented in six settings along an embodiment gradient, from chat questions about an imagined robot to closed-loop control of a simulated robot arm. Benign controls, safe-alternative variants and scripted operator pushback complement each task. Across six open- and closed-weight VLMs and 11,480 episodes, hazardous-action rates rise from 14% in chat to 47% in the simulator, and from 2% to 80% for the most affected model. The increase is largely driven by open-weight models. We find that models flag hazards before acting in 73% of unsafe episodes and give way to pushback about twice as often when controlling robots as in chat. The safest models also show signs of overcaution on benign controls. Safety evaluations run in text therefore do not predict the safety behavior of the same models when used as robot controllers.

paper_title: LeCellModel: Interpretable Density Estimation over the Gene Expression Manifold
paper_abstract: Representation learning for single-cell RNA-seq has been evaluated by the identities representations capture -- cell types, lineages, perturbations -- rather than how faithfully they model the distribution of cell states on the gene expression manifold. As a result, density estimation, rare-state detection, perturbation scoring, and gene-level attribution are bolted onto frozen embeddings as separate models, disconnected from the geometry of the data. We argue that modeling the distribution of cell states should be the primary objective, and that representation quality follows from it. Building on LeJEPA, whose SIGReg objective enforces a provably optimal isotropic Gaussian latent, we introduce LeCellModel, which reads the encoder's Jacobian log-volume (JEPA-SCORE) under this Gaussian latent as a relative typicality score. Across several datasets, LeCellModel outperforms established methods on the scIB benchmark for representation quality. Furthermore, we show that LeCellModel enables detection of rare expression states using JEPA-SCORE as a typicality measure, applying it to a controlled cytokine panel, where it identifies stimulated cells across minority fractions and tracks pathway-response magnitude. We introduce gene-level interpretability of the typicality score -- to our knowledge, the first method for analyzing JEPA-SCORE in feature space. Leveraging this framework, LeCellModel recapitulates the known association of a profibrotic macrophage program with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and discovers a CD177+ activated regulatory T cell subpopulation previously described only in tumor contexts. Both findings emerge directly from the geometry of the learned embedding, without relying on supervised annotations.

paper_title: Evaluable Language-Model Treatment Policies for Sepsis Resuscitation via Offline Value-Guided Selection
paper_abstract: Offline treatment learning must balance imitation, which stays close to logged evidence but ignores outcomes, against value maximisation, which uses outcomes but drifts toward treatments the records cannot verify. Numerical reinforcement learning strikes this balance during training. For large language models (LLMs), directly using sparse retrospective outcomes for fine-tuning raises challenges of delayed credit assignment and limited evidence for alternative treatments. We present R-LLMC, which strikes the balance at inference for sepsis resuscitation. A behaviour-supervised LLM, decoded into an exact distribution over 25 vasopressor-fluid actions, proposes clinician-anchored candidates; an offline critic selects among them by estimated long-term value. The policy has a closed form for off-policy evaluation, and its rationale is written after selection, so explanation cannot steer treatment. In experiments on held-out MIMIC-III patients, R-LLMC exceeded the clinician reference in doubly robust value by +0.214 (95\% CI 0.091-0.300), with fitted Q evaluation agreeing.

paper_title: SIAMBA: A Pseudo-Siamese Mamba-based Deep Learning Network for Multimodal Flood Change Detection
paper_abstract: Flood change detection from bi-temporal multispectral and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images is essential for rapid disaster response. In this context, Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery provides discriminative spectral observations, whereas Sentinel-1 SAR provides weather-independent structural information. Using these modalities jointly requires modelling temporal evidence while accounting for cross-modal heterogeneity. In particular, change detection is complicated by cloud contamination, illumination variability, acquisition geometry and speckle, and heterogeneous land-cover responses. To address these challenges, we propose SIAMBA, a pseudo-siamese Mamba-based network for bi-temporal flood change detection from paired Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 observations. SIAMBA uses dedicated modality-specific encoders with dual-pooling squeeze-and-excitation recalibration and selective state-space processing for long-range spatial context. A gated cross-modal change module derives absolute, signed, and relative log-ratio differences at multiple semantic levels, and attention-refined skip connections support progressive multi-scale decoding. Experiments are carried out on OMBRIA benchmark, which includes an independent test set and geographically diverse subsets in France, Albania, Guyana, and Timor. SIAMBA achieves 81.98% IoU, and 93.57% OA on the independent test set, reaching the highest values in the considered comparison. It also provides the highest unweighted average IoU and OA across four regional subsets spatially disjuncted. These results indicate that combining selective state-space contextual modelling with gated multiscale discrepancy learning effectively improves flood change mapping across the evaluated geographic settings.
comments: 9 pages, 3 figures, presented at SPIE Environmental Remote Sensing, 2026

paper_title: PRIMEAPE: A Multilingual Benchmark for Fine-Grained Meta-Evaluation of Judge Models
paper_abstract: Large language models increasingly serve as judges of other models, shaping benchmark rankings and model development. Yet, a judge whose rationale consistently supports its verdict may still disagree with human preferences. To study this, we introduce PRIMEAPE, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating judge verdicts and rationales. PRIMEAPE provides 2,205 response pairs covering 243 instructions in English, French, Spanish, Urdu, Hindi, Norwegian Bokmål, and Yoruba, with 11k human annotations of preferences and rationales across relevance, naturalness, truthfulness, safety, and overall quality. Our evaluation of twelve open- and closed-weight judges reveals that aggregate performance conceals differences across languages and criteria, while requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences. Judges also favor the first position, longer responses, and responses from related models, with effects that vary across criteria and languages. Crucially, judges can justify verdicts that disagree with human preferences while maintaining consistency between their verdicts and rationales. These findings show that consistency with a judge's own verdict does not establish alignment with human judgment. PRIMEAPE enables assessment of both, providing a foundation for more reliable multilingual judges. We release our benchmark and all annotation materials under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license at github.com/Toloka/primeape.

paper_title: TrialAgentBench: Evaluating AI Agents for Clinical-Trial Analysis and Long-Horizon Drug-Development Decisions
paper_abstract: Clinical drug development is a long-horizon, high-stakes process requiring sequential decisions based on information that costs money and time to acquire. AI agents have demonstrated capabilities for scientific analysis, but there is no established way to evaluate them on these decisions, as real trials are expensive, involve people, and never reveal the counterfactual. We introduce TrialAgentBench, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on clinical trial analysis and drug development decision-making using simulated trials where the truth is known, embedded within the data records of a fictional drug sponsor. We publicly release nearly 3,500 tasks, varying from analysing a single trial to managing multi-phase programmes with budget and time constraints. We score each analysis by rerunning its code on new trials, and each programme by the value its decisions achieve. Across 24 closed- and open-weight models, the strongest agents can analyse raw, messy trial records to within 6% of a process-aware analysis, even when an assumption is violated, with 95% confidence intervals containing the true effect 94--95% of the time. Over the prior year, the best model improved from 19% above this analysis, with serious misses on 15% of tasks, to 3.5% and 1%. What limits them is decision-making from evidence under uncertainty: when to correct, what evidence to buy, when to stop. The strongest agents are overly careful, correcting on 83% of tasks with equal recording errors, where it is unnecessary. On drug programmes, the best agent has substantial headroom, reaching 48% of the value an oracle achieves against 58% for a rule-based developer, with others falling 24 to 66% short. Model generations show ongoing improvements in handling data and evidence, with substantial variation. The strongest models can act as competent analysts, but do not yet make reliable long-horizon decisions.

paper_title: Do Waste Classifiers Recognise Items They Have Never Seen? Object-Disjoint Evaluation on Household and Medical Waste
paper_abstract: Automatic waste classification supports source separation, which enables recycling and keeps hazardous medical items out of household waste. Waste classification studies often report near-perfect accuracy on random image splits, which put photographs of one item in both training and test sets. To measure how well classifiers recognise items they have never seen, we built BanglaWaste-23, with 4,160 images of 172 objects in 23 household and medical waste classes from Bangladesh. Every image also records which physical item it shows. We evaluated 11 ImageNet-pretrained models and two models trained from scratch (a compact custom network and MobileNetV3-L) using object-disjoint five-fold cross-validation and a random split. On unseen objects, the best pretrained model reached a macro-averaged F1 score of 98.8%, and six models were statistically tied. The random split overstated from-scratch accuracy by 15 to 19 percentage points. The from-scratch models also missed 11 to 13% of medical items, against under 1% for pretrained models. On a second dataset from Dhaka, pretrained accuracy fell by 15 to 22 points. Classifiers should therefore be evaluated on unseen objects, with random-split results read as an upper bound. The data are on Zenodo and the code at https://github.com/saadbaust/BanglaWaste-23.

paper_title: Replay Before You Reply: Second-Look Prompting for Unified Multimodal Encoding
paper_abstract: Solving multimodal tasks requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to form a unified understanding of the image and the question text. However, under causal attention in current VLMs, a token can attend only to what precedes it. Whichever modality comes first is therefore encoded under partial observation of the input, uninformed by the rest of the multimodal context. We introduce Second-Look Prompting (SLP), a training-free method that repeats the image-question pair in the input. In the repeated copy, every visual and textual token can attend to the complete input, yielding a unified multimodal encoding of the pair. Moreover, the added visual tokens contribute computation beyond re-exposing the image: even a blank image in their place can improve reasoning. Across 12 benchmarks, SLP improves the overall average score of every evaluated model, spanning nine open-source models (3B-72B) and three proprietary frontier models, with gains reaching 5.6 points for Gemini 3 Flash on MATH-Vision. Our analysis reveals two complementary mechanisms: the question guides where the second image attends, and the added visual tokens act as a prefill scratchpad whose hidden states retain answer-relevant information from the image and question. These findings highlight input presentation as a simple yet effective way to improve VLM performance.

paper_title: World Models as Native Latent Action Models
paper_abstract: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.
comments: 19 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Project page: https://pawteam-eai.github.io/native-lam/
