Few studies have looked at how to detect forged degree certificates, partly because public benchmarks are scarce. We present TamperCert, a benchmark built from 400 real degree certificates issued by 38 universities. Each certificate was subjected to 11 publicly available tampering methods to alter the holder's name and further processed with four additional post-processing techniques, resulting in over 20,000 forged images. We evaluate 13 detectors, a commercial multimodal large language model (MLLM), and detectors trained on TamperCert.Our findings reveal that no detector is reliable for every tampering method. Consequently, a determined forger may still evade detection. Moreover, the commercial MLLM misses most forgeries made by general-purpose generative models, and post-processing, such as resizing an image or photographing it with a camera, severely degrades detection.

paper_title: Optimistic Online Learning for Coding Agents with Aggregate Feedback
paper_abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents operating on Web development platforms can interact with repositories, issue trackers, and continuous integration services to carry out long-horizon software engineering tasks. However, behavioral drift remains a major bottleneck in such multi-turn reasoning and action trajectories. To mitigate this, activation steering has emerged as a promising approach for regularizing agent behaviors by intervening on the LLM's transformer residual streams. Nonetheless, existing methods typically apply a static steering policy across all tasks, overlooking the fact that a single policy is rarely effective across heterogeneous tasks and varying execution turns. This limitation motivates dynamic online selection among candidate steering policies. Yet, doing so in long-horizon agentic settings is challenging: verifiable task-level feedback is only revealed upon task completion, leaving the contributions of individual steering turns unobserved. To address this challenge, we formulate online steering-policy selection as a multi-armed bandit problem with delayed task-level feedback and turn-level predictive hints derived from residual-stream activations. Within this formulation, we introduce Online Optimistic Activation Steering, a meta-framework that uses hints to guide within-task steering policy selection and leverages terminal task-level feedback to correct cumulative reward estimates. Theoretically, against the best fixed policy in hindsight, we prove regret bounds that tighten with increasing hint accuracy and establish a matching lower bound with respect to prediction error and candidate policy count. Empirical evaluations on realistic coding benchmarks demonstrate that our framework outperforms both static steering policies and naive online adaptive baselines.

paper_title: Toward a Scalable and Adaptive Evaluation Measure for Time Series Anomaly Detection
paper_abstract: Time Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) is a fundamental task for time series analytics. Unlike other domains, where anomaly detection mainly focuses on point-based anomalies, TSAD must also handle range-based anomalies. Nevertheless, TSAD methods are commonly evaluated with measures inherited from classification, such as Precision and Recall, which require a threshold, or with threshold-independent ones, such as AUC, which ignore the temporal aspect of anomalies. To address these issues, the Volume Under the Surface (VUS) measure scores detectors across all thresholds and a range of buffer lengths and has been widely adopted. However, VUS has two limitations. First, VUS is computationally expensive, requiring 7 hours and 38 minutes to evaluate 32 detectors on the 870 TSB-AD time series. Second, VUS applies the same buffer lengths to every anomaly and detector, which can yield over-optimistic scores that hinder discrimination between accurate and mediocre detectors. We first introduce FastVUS, which computes VUS exactly and on average 76x faster by (i) computing all buffers in parallel, (ii) pruning irrelevant buffers for the existence reward, (iii) casting the confusion matrix as a single reduced matrix multiplication, (iv) computing VUS for every buffer length in one pass, and (v) discarding non-anomalous regions with a global mask. We also develop FastVUS-GPU, which recasts every step as batched tensor operations and reaches an average 304x speedup with a maximum error of $5\times10^{-3}$. Building on FastVUS, we introduce AutoVUS, an adaptive extension that compares each detection against a random baseline and selects the buffer length that maximizes the gain over it. Our case studies show that AutoVUS reduces over-optimistic scores and better separates accurate from mediocre detectors. We release FastVUS and AutoVUS as open source to promote time-aware evaluation at scale.

paper_title: mini-psych-agent: Evaluating Human-Like Behavior in LLM Agents through Interactive Psychological Environments
paper_abstract: A Large Language Model (LLM), its harness, and the test-time compute budget jointly determine its behavior. Consequently, the same underlying model, embedded in different agentic workflows or allocated different amounts of test-time compute, can exhibit markedly different performance. Psychologists face an analogous challenge when evaluating human performance: the same person may behave differently under different incentives and levels of deliberation. Psychological tasks therefore provide an ideal testbed for studying such behavioral variation. However, when adapted to LLMs, these tasks are typically text-transcribed, replaying fixed, language-rendered experiments as static prompts. This format is ill-suited to agent evaluation, where actions can alter future observations and task states. Conversely, although dynamic environments are prevalent in the evaluation of LLM agents, they rarely ask whether the resulting behavior is human-like. Here, we bridge this gap by transforming psychological tasks into dynamic environments in which agents can interact and by using a learned human-policy model to evaluate how compatible the resulting behavioral trajectories are with human behavior. Across these environments, we find that this compatibility varies with an LLM's agentic configuration and the psychological task, and that memory raises it mainly by making choices more predictable rather than more human-like. These findings motivate a more holistic evaluation of LLM agents in psychology-inspired environments, accounting for both the backbone model and its agentic scaffold.

paper_title: Boosting zero-shot learning through neuro-symbolic integration
paper_abstract: Zero-shot learning (ZSL) aims to train deep neural networks to recognize objects from unseen classes, starting from a semantic description of the concepts. Neuro-symbolic (NeSy) integration refers to a class of techniques that incorporate symbolic knowledge representation and reasoning with the learning capabilities of deep neural networks. However, to date, few studies have explored how to leverage NeSy techniques to inject prior knowledge during the training process to boost ZSL capabilities. Here, we present Fuzzy Logic Prototypical Network (FLPN) that formulates the classification task as prototype matching in a visual-semantic embedding space, which is trained by optimizing a NeSy loss. Specifically, FLPN exploits the Logic Tensor Network (LTN) framework to incorporate background knowledge in the form of logical axioms by grounding a first-order logic language as differentiable operations between real tensors. This prior knowledge includes class hierarchies (classes and macroclasses) along with robust high-level inductive biases. The latter allow, for instance, to handle exceptions in class-level attributes and to enforce similarity between images of the same class, preventing premature overfitting to seen classes and improving overall performance. % CHECK: original sentence had no verb ("Both class-level and attribute-level prototypes through an attention mechanism ...") FLPN learns both class-level and attribute-level prototypes, the latter through an attention mechanism specialized for either convolutional- or transformer-based backbones. FLPN achieves state-of-the-art performance on the GZSL benchmarks AWA2 and SUN, matching or exceeding the performance of competing algorithms with minimal computational overhead. The code is available at https://github.com/FrancescoManigrass/FLPN

paper_title: STAR: Structure-Aware Temporal Action Recovery for Point Supervised Temporal Action Localization
paper_abstract: Point supervised temporal action localization is becoming the need of time in this era of ever growing and non-stop video data. Existing method mainly rely on snippet level action response to generate pseudo labels. However, these labels often suffer from boundary ambiguity, over extended proposals, and weak temporal structure. To address these issues, we propose STAR, a structure-aware Temporal Action Recovery framework for point supervised temporal action localization. STAR works by enhancing the base S model with temporal difference interaction with attention module to capture forward and backward snippet changes, and introduces the learning of start, core, and end roles to model the internal temporal structure of actions. In addition, STAR further improves the pseudo label generation through All point proposal ranking and Rolebank based structural re-ranking, which suppress neighbor crossing and structurally inconsistent proposals. Finally, temporal action detector to STAR feedback supervision transfers high quality detector prediction back to the STAR model through soft start, core, end, action, and background targets. This helps to further refine the pseudo labels. Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks shows the effectiveness of STAR. By using I3D features, STAR achieves 67.2% at AVG@0.1:0.7 on THUMOS'14, 58.1% on GTEA, 74.6% on BEOID, and 31.7% at AVG@0.5:0.95 on ActivityNet-1.3, outperforming previous point supervised methods across multiple benchmarks.

paper_title: RepoClean: Evaluating Coding Agents on Repository-Level Obsolete Code Cleanup
paper_abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong repository-level programming capabilities. However, as software evolves, repository code may become redundant or obsolete, increasing maintenance costs and potentially introducing functional issues. Agents must therefore identify and remove unnecessary code safely, yet autonomous repository-level code cleanup remains insufficiently evaluated in isolation. To evaluate this capability, we introduce RepoClean, a benchmark of 200 cleanup tasks from 34 popular open-source Python repositories. RepoClean is constructed by automatically reintroducing deleted code from real repository histories into newer versions, preserving current implementations and retaining instances where previously passing tests consequently fail. To restore existing functionality without new feature development, agents must use repository interfaces and cross-file dependencies to determine which historical code to remove and which implementations to preserve. Evaluation of seven models shows that even the best-performing model, GPT-6 Astra, resolves only 23% of tasks. Further analysis reveals that agents remove substantially less obsolete code when cleanup is not explicitly requested. RepoClean provides a foundation for systematically studying these cleanup challenges and advancing coding agents toward autonomous software maintenance.

paper_title: Shift by Analogy for Compositional Zero-Shot Learning
paper_abstract: Compositional zero-shot learning recognizes attribute-object pairs absent from training. An unseen pair has a semantic description but lacks an observed visual reference. We propose Shift by Analogy (SBA) to make unseen compositions visually seen through a shift-then-match process. Its core add-subtract-add rule transfers an attribute change between two seen image-text residuals on a source object to a reference residual on the target object. This shifts the target's own text feature toward its visual center; learned refinement produces a proxy for matching query images. During training, each target is excluded from its supports, and recognition is learned using references constructed from other pairs. An analogy library and same-object attention extend this construction across candidates, while joint learning integrates proxy matching with semantic and primitive evidence. Visual-center analysis confirms substantially improved correspondence for unseen compositions. Experiments across three standard benchmarks show that SBA consistently outperforms strong CZSL baselines under both closed- and open-world evaluation.

paper_title: FMSNO: Scaling Surface Neural Operators by Learned Flow Matching Reparametrisation
paper_abstract: We propose the Flow Matching Surface Neural Operator (FMSNO), which combines learning a shared map from irregular surface meshes to a regular two-dimensional grid on the sphere and training a neural operator on the regular grid. Constructing a separate map for each new geometry can dominate inference time on large meshes. We initially pretrain the mapping by flow matching using precomputed optimal transport maps as targets and then continue its training using combined geometry and CFD objectives. We apply it to unseen geometries in a single forward pass. The learned flow deforms the surface points, and we project its endpoints onto the sphere. We then splat geometric features onto the spherical grid, apply a neural operator (we tested both Fourier and Spherical Fourier Neural Operators), and interpolate its output back to the surface. For a mesh with $N$ points, evaluating the map costs O(N), and the full prediction costs O(NlogN) with the FNO backbone. We evaluate surface pressure prediction on ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, and drag coefficient prediction on DrivAerNet++. Across the three pressure benchmarks, our accuracy is on par with that of the most accurate baseline. On a surface with one million points, our method achieves a 354x end-to-end inference speedup over that baseline while keeping the same memory usage asymptotics of O(N).

paper_title: AirVT-15k: A Query-Diverse UAV Video-Text Dataset and Query-Adaptive Evidence Alignment Network for Retrieval
paper_abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle video-text retrieval (UAV-TVR) requires matching language to both scene context and subtle object changes. A harbor-layout query relies on global scene context, whereas a departing-vessel query requires local functional cues and motion states. Existing benchmarks provide diverse aerial descriptions but give limited attention to distinct evidence needs within the same video. We introduce AirVT-15k, a benchmark of 15,504 UAV videos and 155,040 captions, with ten complementary bilingual captions per video describing scenes, object states, and temporal changes. We also propose AirFocus-CST, which selects query-relevant frames and patches, encodes temporal feature differences, and combines coarse-to-fine interaction (CFI) with optimal-transport alignment (OTA). Average mean recall reaches 63.67% on AirVT-15k and 24.41% on CapERA, improving over the strongest baselines by 2.96 and 1.91 percentage points, respectively. The dataset and code are available at https://chenxi000233.github.io/AirVT-15k-site/.

paper_title: Learning Teacher Output Preferences from Final Responses for Reasoning Distillation
paper_abstract: Many large language models (LLMs) use chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve complex problems, but hide their CoT traces to prevent reasoning capabilities from being distilled. While recent studies have shown that hidden CoTs can be reconstructed, existing methods typically require training a separate attacker for each target LLM. This paper studies model-agnostic CoT reconstruction, aiming to reconstruct hidden CoT traces from arbitrary target LLMs using only input prompts and visible final responses. We propose Final-Output Preference Learning (FOPL), which trains a single reconstruction model that generalizes to unseen LLMs without target-specific adaptation. To achieve this, the reconstruction model must learn which reasoning patterns match a given final response without knowing the target LLM's identity. We address this using preference optimization, training the reconstruction model to prefer native CoTs over synthetic alternatives for the same question and final response. By learning these preferences from LLMs with accessible CoTs, the reconstruction model learns to distinguish reasoning patterns based on visible responses. Experiments show that reconstructed CoTs capture distinct reasoning patterns across LLM families, including a family unseen during training. Moreover, students trained on reconstructed CoTs match or outperform those trained on native CoTs across several reasoning benchmarks.

paper_title: MH-RAG-DIVE: Dynamic and Cost-Efficient Multi-Hop RAG Evaluation via Tree-Cached Dialogue Simulation
paper_abstract: Quality assessment is essential for determining whether changes to a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system improve or maintain its performance. However, existing evaluation approaches often rely on single-turn or single-hop interactions and therefore do not capture the complexity of multi-hop, multi-turn conversations. We introduce MH-RAG-DIVE, a dynamic interactive user simulation framework designed to evaluate RAG systems in more complex multi-hop and multi-turn settings. The framework extends RAG-DIVE with a Context Discoverer, which identifies documents that can be combined to generate multi-hop questions within an ongoing conversation. To address the high computational cost of dynamic user simulation, we further introduce a Conversation Cacher, which reuses turns from previous evaluation runs while preserving the dynamic nature of the evaluation. We evaluate the framework across six distinct RAG configurations and compare its results with the original RAG-DIVE evaluation and the static, human-created CLAPNQ dataset. Our experiments show consistent performance trends across the evaluation approaches, while the more complex multi-hop and multi-turn setting exposes additional challenges for RAG systems. Furthermore, the Conversation Cacher substantially reduces token consumption, demonstrating its potential to make dynamic evaluation more cost-efficient. Finally, we apply MH-RAG-DIVE to an industrial RAG system with domain-specific data, demonstrating its applicability to real-world evaluation scenarios. Overall, our results show that the proposed approach provides a more complex and cost-efficient framework for evaluating RAG systems. All code and experimental data are publicly available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/Daniel-Innsbruck/MH-RAG-DIVE).
comments: This preprint was accepted for presentation at the 19th International Conference on Agents and Artificial Intelligence (ICAART27)

paper_title: Verifiable On-Policy Distillation
paper_abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful approach for improving language-model reasoning, but its supervision is inherently sparse: a sequence-level verifier reward is propagated only through sampled trajectories and provides no direct signal for alternative actions. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a complementary form of supervision by providing dense teacher feedback over the full next-token distribution, but this signal is not grounded in verified task outcomes. Simply co-optimizing the two objectives does not couple these signals: verifier feedback remains sparse and does not inform the dense teacher supervision. We introduce Verifiable On-Policy Distillation (VOPD), which transfers sparse verifier feedback into dense, verifier-grounded supervision. Our key observation is that the implicit-reward view of OPD places teacher supervision and verifier feedback in a common reward space while retaining a reward signal available for every next-token action. Under this view, VOPD projects verifier preference onto the teacher's implicit-reward direction and Rao--Blackwellizes the resulting signal over the full vocabulary, propagating verifier-grounded supervision to actions that were never sampled. The resulting objective can also be interpreted as adaptively extrapolating the distillation target according to teacher--verifier agreement. Across two teacher--student configurations and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VOPD consistently improves both final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy distillation baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/juntongshi48/VOPD.

paper_title: Video Generalized Category Discovery
paper_abstract: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to categorize unlabeled data from both known and unknown classes using labeled data from only the known classes. While recent GCD methods have shown promise on static images, their performance degrades in videos due to temporal dynamics, larger intra-class variation, and the lack of temporal consistency in existing approaches. We introduce VideoGCD, a framework tailored for video action recognition under the GCD setting. Our method integrates (i) a partitioned Mixture-of-Experts module that encourages specialization for known and novel categories, (ii) a novel-class balancing loss to reduce bias toward known classes, and (iii) a temporal optimal transport loss that promotes consistent routing across frames. Experiments on three video benchmarks demonstrate that VideoGCD significantly improves performance over existing GCD methods, particularly on novel categories. Our findings highlight the importance of combining temporal modeling and expert specialization for video GCD.

paper_title: SafeRank-ReID: Candidate-Conditioned Re-Ranking under Identity Conflicts for Multimodal Person Re-Identification
paper_abstract: Multimodal Person Re-Identification (ReID) exploits complementary identity cues from different sensing modalities to mitigate the performance degradation caused by challenging imaging conditions. Existing methods typically estimate Modality Reliability at the query level, making it difficult to identify conflicting inputs that retain normal visual quality but correspond to an incorrect identity. Such inputs may receive high confidence, promote irrelevant gallery candidates, and lead to negative fusion. To address this issue, we propose SafeRank-ReID, a candidate-conditioned safe re-ranking framework for Multimodal Person Re-Identification (ReID). To capture the varying support of the same modality for different candidates, we introduce a candidate-conditioned evidence arbitration mechanism that integrates unimodal retrieval evidence, input quality, and cross-modal consistency to estimate trust and conflict logits for each modality-candidate pair. Together, these logits contribute to the normalized modality weights, allowing support strength to vary across modalities and candidates while reducing the contribution of potentially unreliable evidence. A candidate-set refinement module subsequently applies self-attention to jointly model candidate representations and predicts residual scores from their competitive relations, thereby refining the initial fused ranking. For fusion results that remain uncertain after refinement, a query-level fallback gate estimates an interpolation coefficient from the overall conflict level and cross-modal uncertainty, adaptively combining the fused scores with those of the most reliable unimodal branch. Experiments on RGBNT201 and MSVR310 show that SafeRank-ReID maintains competitive clean-input retrieval while improving robustness to Identity Conflicts across person and vehicle benchmarks.
comments: Accepted at ACM Multimedia Asia 2026 (MMAsia 2026). 8 pages, 5 figures

paper_title: PinGround: Pinning Queries to Points for Parallel Grounding in Vision-Language Models
paper_abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can localize through their text interface, grounding open-vocabulary objects, complex referring expressions, text lines and layout regions with strong semantic understanding. They write the boxes one after another as a single sequence, although the instances of a query, unlike the words of a sentence, form an unordered set with no sequential dependence. The number of decoding steps therefore grows with the number of instances, which makes dense scenes the most expensive. Decoding the instances in parallel avoids this growth, but streams that cannot see each other duplicate some instances and miss others. We propose \method, which writes a single point into each query as a spatial anchor and asks for the matching instance nearest to that point within a local radius, or \none. Given the image, the anchored queries are independent, so they are decoded in parallel as leaves of a prefix tree that shares the image and the query, and the model is trained on the same tree. Coarse-to-fine anchors refine only the regions where instances are found, duplicate suppression keeps one box per instance, and set-level reinforcement learning optimizes the set F1. Only the prompt and the attention mask change, not the architecture. On three different VLMs and 12 benchmarks covering detection, OCR, layout and referring, \method is at most 5.5 F1 below sequential decoding trained on the same data, while its speedup grows with instance density and reaches 21.9$\times$ on dense scenes.

paper_title: HEART: Hierarchical Expert Adaptive Refinement Transformer for ECG Representation Learning
paper_abstract: Learning robust representations from electrocardiograms (ECGs) is challenging because repeated cardiac cycles coexist with subtle and sparse diagnostic cues in local morphology and rhythm-level context. Existing ECG foundation models commonly rely on Transformerbased patch encoders with uniformly shared dense refinement pathways, limiting adaptive processing across heterogeneous ECG tokens. We propose HEART (Hierarchical Expert Adaptive Refinement Transformer), an ECG foundation model that introduces stage-specific conditional expert refinement during self-supervised pre-training. HEART places a local-level MoE over patch-level representations before temporal contextualization and a global-level MoE over context-integrated token representations after self-attention. Token-level Top-1 routing allows different patches or contextual tokens within the same ECG to follow different expert pathways. On public ECG benchmarks, HEART achieves strong performance under both linear probing and fine-tuning, with particularly large frozen-encoder gains on PTB-XL Form and Rhythm (+6.76 AUROC points each over the strongest protocol-reproduced baseline). Routing analyses provide qualitative evidence of complementary local and global expert specialization. We release our code and pretrained models at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/HEART-5E9F.

paper_title: Topology-Prior-Guided Regional Latent Dynamics for Transient Structural Response Prediction
paper_abstract: Predicting the transient nonlinear responses of complex engineering structures remains challenging due to large finite element meshes, heterogeneous structural components, and history-dependent mechanical behavior. This study proposes a topology-prior-guided regional latent dynamics (TPLD) surrogate model that combines physically structured regional representations with dynamics-aware latent learning for full-field time-history prediction. Based on mesh topology and engineering priors, structural responses are encoded into spatially coupled regional latent variables through region-aware feature extraction and topology-constrained interactions. An auxiliary one-step prediction task enhances latent-space dynamical predictability by introducing state-transition supervision. A load-conditioned spatiotemporal Mamba model then predicts regional latent trajectories by integrating temporal causal scanning and bidirectional spatial scanning, while a shared coordinate-conditioned decoder reconstructs full-field nodal responses. The framework is evaluated on three finite element datasets: a parametric stiffened panel, a partitioned pressure impact plate, and a Toyota Yaris full-vehicle crash model. The relative L2 errors for the three displacement components range from 4.00% to 8.21% on the stiffened panel and from 1.41% to 12.22% on the approximately 1.49-million-node vehicle model. On the BIW crash benchmark, TPLD achieves a relative L2 position error of 0.620%, representing a 30.7% reduction compared with the best-performing GeoTransolver configuration. Ablation studies demonstrate the advantages of topology-guided regional representations over global latent and learnable soft-slice alternatives, while auxiliary one-step prediction particularly improves the prediction of accumulated plastic strain.

paper_title: Temporal Leakage Distorts the TGB Node Affinity Leaderboard: A Point-in-Time Audit
paper_abstract: Node affinity prediction in the Temporal Graph Benchmark (TGB) asks how a node's future interactions will be distributed over other nodes. On this task, methods that reuse past ground-truth labels often outperform temporal graph neural networks, and the state of the art builds on them. Such comparisons assume a point-in-time correct evaluation, in which a model receives only information available at prediction time. Drawing on as-of joins and bitemporal databases, we formalize this requirement by distinguishing when a label must be predicted, its query time, from when it is fully determined, its availability time, and we audit the four TGB node affinity datasets and their evaluation loop with model-agnostic tools. None of the four meets it. On three datasets, each label summarizes a single day about five days after its timestamp, not the documented following week, yet the loop feeds it back right after that timestamp; on the fourth, the loop processes the edges from which each label is computed before predicting it. Under a drop-in leakage-free protocol, every method whose inputs leak loses up to 17% of its NDCG@10, the advantage of past labels over the interaction stream nearly vanishes or reverses, and both the best configuration of the state of the art and the rankings change; a blend of training-free long-memory statistics, with weights fit on validation data, matches or exceeds the state of the art under both protocols. Point-in-time correctness should therefore be built into benchmarks, and our tools carry over to other benchmarks whose labels aggregate event streams over time windows.

paper_title: Face Is Not All You Need: MIME Benchmark for Incomplete Multimodal Emotion Recognition
paper_abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) is a fundamental task in multimedia understanding, where state-of-the-art methods have achieved prominent success relying on the assumption of complete, well-aligned multimodal inputs. However, real-world unconstrained scenarios often suffer from unpredictable modality degradation and information loss, leading to catastrophic performance collapse of existing MER models that heavily depend on facial cues as the core inference anchor. However, few systematic works evaluate model robustness under diverse, fine-grained incomplete settings, as prior works are limited to coarse-grained full-modality removal and neglect interpretable analysis of emotional reasoning. To bridge this gap, we formally define the Incomplete Multimodal Emotion Recognition (IMER) task, which benchmarks model generalization and robustness under multi-grained modality and emotional information loss. We further construct MIME, a dedicated IMER benchmark with 2,000 video segments covering realistic fine-grained facial-detail degradation, severe facial degradation, and extreme full-modality loss, surpassing the limited coarse-grained settings of prior works. We also propose the Chain of Emotion (CoE) analysis paradigm with tailored metrics to dissect the fine-grained emotional cue perception and reasoning process of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Extensive experiments on seven mainstream MLLMs reveal that body language and scene context act as critical compensatory mechanisms under facial degradation, while a pronounced gap exists between models' basic visual perception ability and high-level cognitive reasoning. Our work provides a focused evaluation platform and actionable insights for advancing robust multimodal emotion recognition. Our dataset and code are public at https://yuxinokk.github.io/MIME.
comments: Published in the Proceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM '26), November 10--14, 2026, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

paper_title: MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation
paper_abstract: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.

paper_title: Seeing Is Not Acting: WARD Diagnoses the Evidence-to-State-to-Action Gap in Longitudinal Clinical Agents
paper_abstract: Large language models for longitudinal clinical care must revise their assessments and actions as patient information accumulates. However, benchmarks centered on isolated responses or final task outcomes provide limited insight into intermediate failures in evidence use, state updating, and action selection. We introduce WARD, a benchmark for evaluating how clinical agents translate accumulating evidence into patient-state judgments and timely, safe actions. WARD comprises 4,560 clinical tasks across seven clinical output domains, organized into 240 checkpoints from 40 longitudinal clinical trajectories spanning 95 hospitalizations. Its Longitudinal Track evaluates these tasks under controlled cumulative evidence. Its Interactive Track evaluates end-to-end, tool-mediated clinical management across 271 verifiable evidence items and 141 reference transitions. Across 12 models with scorable checkpoint outputs, evidence recognition consistently outpaces downstream state and action decisions, with linked-evidence nonresponse reaching 74.47--90.90\%. Models also struggle to retain and update information over time, while in the Interactive Track only 11.46\% of executed actions advance a reference transition. These results reveal a persistent evidence-to-state-to-action gap and highlight the need for process-level evaluation of longitudinal clinical agents.Code and data: https://github.com/Dingsuper-creator/WARD.

paper_title: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds
paper_abstract: AI-driven game development holds the potential to transform diverse human inspirations into interactive experiences. However, existing systems and benchmarks primarily focus on explicit development specifications, with limited support for adapting multimodal references and evaluating actual gameplay experiences. We introduce GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform that transforms multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to support continuous refinement. We further present GameAnything-Bench, a benchmark spanning diverse reference modalities, game creation objectives, and gaming environments, with exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations reveal that current agents can adapt reference content but still struggle with playable interactions and precise modifications. Moreover, multimodal references improve content fidelity, while iterative refinement yields substantial but varying improvements across agents. These findings highlight both the potential and remaining challenges of inspiration-driven game development.

paper_title: Complementary Geometry in Gaussian Splatting
paper_abstract: Gaussian Splatting has achieved high visual quality in novel view synthesis, but the accuracy of its rendered geometry remains a challenge. In particular, the rendered depth is computed as an opacity-weighted average along each ray, which may not correspond to the actual scene surface. In this paper, we observe that depth predictions from different views of the same frozen Gaussian representation exhibit complementary errors, allowing us to improve novel-view geometry using information from other views without modifying the original representation. Based on this observation, we propose REVEAL, a general framework that selectively refines novel-view depth using complementary geometric information. Specifically, we first reproject depth predictions from source views to the target view and combine them using robust multi-view consensus. We then introduce a learned selection mechanism to determine whether the candidate depth is more accurate than the original prediction, based on the expected reduction in depth error. In addition, we introduce RIG, a real-world benchmark captured with synchronized RGB-D cameras, which provides ground-truth depth for evaluating both static and dynamic reconstruction models. Experiments on 6 Gaussian Splatting backbones across 3 benchmarks show that REVEAL consistently improves depth accuracy while maintaining comparable rendering quality.

paper_title: DriveTTO: Understanding Search and Selection in Test-Time Trajectory Optimization for End-to-End Driving
paper_abstract: In difficult driving scenes, a learned scorer can select a poor trajectory from a fixed pool even when a better candidate is available. Nearby vehicles and road boundaries can also leave only a narrow range of high-scoring maneuvers. These constraints vary with the scene and are difficult to cover exhaustively during training. We introduce DriveTTO, a training-free method that searches around native proposals and checks each proposed refinement against a retained trajectory. A frozen scorer evaluates completed paths at the endpoints they actually reach, guiding resampling in progressively smaller neighborhoods. From a shared reference, one branch draws on planner proposals and another perturbs vehicle controls. DriveTTO blends their poses at matching times and accepts a branch or fusion update only when both frozen scorers predict a gain. On Navtest, DriveTTO recovers nonzero predictive driver model scores (PDMS) in 51.35% of native zero-score cases on average. Accounting for new failures, the zero-score rate falls from 1.63% to 1.13%. Benchmark-specific configurations achieve 95.54 PDMS and 92.30 extended PDMS (EPDMS) on Navtest, 57.10 EPDMS on Navhard, and 40.1 HD-Score on HUGSIM under observed commands. With a single frozen scorer, DriveTTO-S improves all six evaluated planners on both Navtest and Navhard.
comments: 20 pages, including supplementary material. Project page: https://rtwotwo.github.io/DriveTTO/ Code: https://github.com/Rtwotwo/DriveTTO

paper_title: Unleashing the Value of Raw Point Clouds for 3D Understanding with LLMs
paper_abstract: Standard 3D point cloud language models typically rely on pretrained point encoders to extract 3D features and project them into representations processable by large language models (LLMs). However, these encoders are often originally optimized for pre-defined tasks, resulting in a representation bottleneck that may lead to a substantial mismatch with downstream 3D understanding. Moreover, existing models largely follow a single pass closed-book generation, limiting their ability to actively inspect task-relevant 3D regions or retrieve necessary external knowledge. In this work, we present PointTool, an encoder-free and tool-augmented framework for 3D reasoning. PointTool introduces Alignment-Free Patch Tokenization (AFPT) to locally aggregate raw point clouds while preserving fine-grained geometric structure, and Decoupled Point-Text LoRA (DPL) to facilitate global aggregation and 3D knowledge internalization within a frozen LLM. Building upon these designs, Program-Supervised Tool Reasoning (PSTR) enables the model to explicitly operate on raw 3D data and external resources through executable tools, supporting interactive 3D reasoning grounded in spatial evidence. We further introduce PointCloud-TR, a benchmark comprising 13K 3D objects, 39.8K questions, and 35.6K tool trajectories to facilitate training and evaluation of complex 3D reasoning. Experiments demonstrate that PointTool achieves strong performance on both standard and complex 3D understanding tasks, validating the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
comments: 12 pages, 4 figures. Tailai Chen and Jiawei Yu contributed equally

paper_title: PhyCoVE: Benchmarking Physical Counterfactual Video Editing across Diverse Material Dynamics
paper_abstract: Physical counterfactual video editing turns a source video and a language-specified physical edit at a given execution frame into a counterfactual video that shows how the scene would evolve after the edit. Existing evaluations with counterfactual target videos mainly cover object removal or specific rigid-body motions, although real scenes also involve elastic deformation, fluid flow, and interactions among rigid bodies, elastic solids, and fluids. We introduce PhyCoVE, a benchmark of 533 cases on 110 source videos that covers rigid, elastic, and fluid dynamics in five interaction patterns, with edits that remove an object, change a physical quantity, or insert a new object. For the simulated cases, a language model proposes scene designs, coding agents build them with solvers suited to each material and physically based rendering and then simulate each edit from the source scene state, and humans check every stage. For the real cases, we record continuously from one camera position before and after each edit. We also propose counterfactual fidelity, a metric that applies across materials and their interactions and measures how much of the physical change from the source video to the target video a generated video reproduces. We evaluate seven open-source and commercial video editing models and find that counterfactual fidelity ranks them nearly as human preference does, but even the best model reproduces only about one seventh of the physical change. The models change how a scene looks but rarely how it evolves, whereas a physical edit requires understanding the dynamics that it changes. Physical counterfactual video editing thus remains far from solved, and PhyCoVE provides a foundation for developing and evaluating methods for it.

paper_title: Rateless Lattice Codes over Fading Wiretap Channels: Finite-Length Secrecy and the Secret-Key Capacity of Degraded Sessions
paper_abstract: In rateless transmission the transmitter keeps sending until the legitimate receiver (Bob) can decode. Over a wiretap channel this has a useful side effect: the eavesdropper (Eve) sees only as many symbols as Bob needs, although the transmitter knows neither channel. We study the secrecy of rateless lattice codes in this setting. First, using a public dither and privacy amplification, we prove a finite-length secrecy bound, in total variation distance, for every channel realization, even if Eve knows all codes and seeds and combines all packets. Second, stopping when Bob acknowledges successful decoding, as in hybrid ARQ, costs at most the logarithm of the number of possible feedback outcomes in secret bits. Third, for degraded sessions with state-based stopping and without a pre-shared key or other public discussion, the secret-key rate of a session cannot exceed its accumulated Gaussian secrecy capacity, and adaptive key generation with shaped rateless lattice codes comes within any $ε>0$ of this limit when Eve's channel states are revealed after the session. If only their statistics are known, choosing the key length after the session guarantees a prescribed secrecy-outage probability. Finally, over block Rayleigh fading with a CRC-based acknowledgement and joint belief-propagation decoding, and with Eve $20$~dB weaker on average, the scheme reaches $59$--$69\%$ of the outage-weighted throughput of an ideal infinite-length secure hybrid-ARQ benchmark for Bob SNRs of $8$--$20$~dB.

paper_title: SpatialDuet: Bayesian task routing between a metric expert and a geometry expert for spatial intelligence
paper_abstract: Embodied assistants and wearable devices need 3D spatial reasoning, and their limited hardware restricts them to small vision-language models (VLMs). Small spatial VLMs acquire different abilities from their training: a model trained on large spatial question sets estimates object and room sizes well, whereas a model with a 3D geometry encoder is better at relative directions and absolute distances. Instead of training a single model for all spatial tasks, as published methods do, we build one system that uses each frozen model for the tasks it handles best. We propose SpatialDuet, which pairs a metric expert with a geometry expert under a Bayesian task router. The metric expert is a data-driven spatial VLM run with three training-free modules: training-aligned sampling, metric-aware minimum Bayes risk decoding and per-type metric calibration. The geometry expert is a VLM with a 3D geometry encoder. For each question type, the router estimates from labelled development questions how likely each expert is to be better, and pools their answers with that probability as weight, in log space for numeric answers and over the option distributions for multiple-choice answers. Extensive experiments on four spatial benchmarks covering video and single images validate SpatialDuet; it outperforms the best published small VLMs by 3.17% on VSI-Bench and, excluding a model trained on CV-Bench-style data, by 1.44% on CV-Bench, without training any model weight.

paper_title: Training-Free 3D Editing via Feature-Divergence Localization and Trajectory Correction
paper_abstract: Modifying 3D assets requires enacting targeted structural transformations while strictly preserving the geometric identity of unedited regions. While recent probability flow models enable training-free editing, bounding these modifications within a high-dimensional latent space presents severe mathematical challenges. Current inversion-free trajectories rely on global velocity updates, which often cause spatial bleed into preserved structures and induce trajectory under-commitment, causing edits to stall mid-path. To resolve these dual failures, we introduce FocusFlow, a segmentation-free framework that structures the integration trajectory into two disjoint phases. During early coarse structure formation, FocusFlow applies Feature-Divergence Localization (FDL) to spatially gate the velocity field using intrinsic cross-attention. Once coarse structure has formed, FocusFlow applies Reference Generation Guidance (RGG), a trajectory-correction term that drives convergence to the target shape by pulling the trajectory toward an explicit clean-latent target. Evaluated on the joint Google Scanned Objects and PartObjaverse-Tiny benchmarks, FocusFlow obtains the best preservation scores and the largest edit magnitude among compared methods, suggesting that it can reduce the traditional preservation-modification trade-off. By providing stable, localized geometric control without manual spatial annotations, this phase-scheduled approach lowers technical barriers to the modification of synthetic 3D media.

paper_title: Inclusive Hand Pose Estimation via Topology-Aware Distillation and Progressive Kinematic Reasoning
paper_abstract: Hand pose estimation aims to recover the spatial configuration of hand joints from visual observations and serves as a fundamental perception module for downstream systems that rely on complete and topologically consistent hand representations. Most existing methods are developed under the assumption of fully articulated hand structures and tend to produce unstable or implausible predictions when parts of the kinematic structure are persistently absent, resulting in degraded performance or even system failure despite available partial observations. To study this challenge, we construct IncNYU, a physiologically constrained benchmark that simulates structural incompleteness through morphological modification of complete hand models and retains reference locations for both intact and synthetically removed regions. Based on this benchmark, we propose InsHaPE, an Inclusive Hand Pose Estimation framework designed to remain robust under structural incompleteness while preserving performance on standard, fully articulated hands. Built on hierarchical kinematic modeling, InsHaPE introduces two complementary components. First, a topology-aware distillation strategy transfers joint-level and relational priors from fully articulated hand representations, providing anatomically consistent initialization under missing structures. Second, a progressive kinematic reasoning module performs structured inference along the kinematic chain, enabling complete and anatomically consistent pose estimation under severe structural variations. Extensive experiments on NYU/IncNYU, together with external validation on MSRA, demonstrate that InsHaPE improves robustness under structural incompleteness while maintaining competitive performance on complete hands. System-level evaluations further show that InsHaPE improves robustness for downstream applications that require fixed-topology hand pose representations.
comments: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG)

paper_title: MVAgent: Per-Video Agents under Global Coordination for Multi-Video Understanding
paper_abstract: Multi-video understanding requires systems to combine evidence from different videos for cross-video reasoning. Answering such questions involves two kinds of decisions. Observation decisions must adapt to each video's content, whereas cross-video judgments require relating evidence from different videos based on the question. Most existing agents make both kinds of decisions in one controller, whose context accumulates observations from every video. We separate them in MVAgent, a training-free Multi-Video Understanding Agent framework with one LocalAgent per video. Each LocalAgent plans observations of its own video and keeps a private observation history. A GlobalAgent coordinates cross-video reasoning by instructing the LocalAgents and combining their reports with joint observation. We evaluate MVAgent on CVBench, MVU-Eval, and CrossVid, using three Qwen3.5 models of different sizes and GPT-6-sol. With Qwen3.5, our framework improves aggregate benchmark scores by 5.1 points on average over Single-pass inference with the same model and by 5.0 points over the strongest prior agent using the same model. With GPT-6-sol, the average gain over Single-pass inference with the same model is 4.3 points. On the same hardware, MVAgent also runs 1.8-2.7 times faster than prior agents of comparable size.

paper_title: ATLAS: Autoregressive Trajectories for Longitudinal Analysis of Survival
paper_abstract: Dynamic survival prediction requires estimates that reflect a patient's observed clinical history. We introduce ATLAS (Autoregressive Trajectories for Longitudinal Analysis of Survival), a framework that trains a sequence model on longitudinal data and autoregressively samples possible futures conditional on an individual's covariates and observed history. These trajectories form a patient-specific synthetic cohort from which Kaplan-Meier survival curves and Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence curves are estimated. We evaluate ATLAS using two stochastic finite-state automaton benchmarks with exact conditional reference curves: a single-covariate process with duration dependence and a late rule change, and a three-covariate Markov process with recovery and competing causes of death. Comparisons include eight direct survival models, including validation-optimized DRSA and Dynamic-DeepHit and history-aware SurvTRACE adaptations, with each neural model trained nine times in the first experiment and five times in the second. After baseline, every ATLAS configuration had lower mean survival-curve error than every fitted direct comparator in both experiments. With a common Sobol sampler and 10,000 trajectories per patient, the best ATLAS model did so in every individual training run, and its mean error was 62% to 84% lower than that of the strongest direct comparator. Baseline advantages were smaller and less consistent in the duration-dependent experiment. ATLAS provides a generative framework for history-conditioned survival estimation, while the accompanying benchmarks enable direct assessment of individual survival and competing-risk predictions against known reference curves.
comments: 77 pages, 5 figures in the main text. Includes Appendices A-D and Supplementary Material (Sections S1-S10)

paper_title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images
paper_abstract: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.

paper_title: VeriLogic: Reinforcement Learning over Verifiable Logical Reasoning Traces
paper_abstract: Logical reasoning derives conclusions from premises through explicit intermediate inference steps, providing a natural basis for process-level verification and supervision. However, existing learning methods often rely on response-level outcome signals, which overlook heterogeneous correctness within the reasoning trace: a correct answer may contain invalid reasoning, while valid intermediate steps may also appear in an incorrect response. To address this issue, we introduce Reinforcement Learning on Verifiable Logical Reasoning (VeriLogic), which turns internal reasoning traces into explicit and verifiable learning objects. Rather than treating a response as an indivisible learning unit, VeriLogic decomposes logical reasoning into explicit intermediate judgments, proofs, and final decisions, and organizes them into a unified "Grounding - Optimization - Refinement" pipeline: (1) Verification-Grounded Reasoning Environment Construction grounds logical reasoning into explicit intermediate states and formally checkable proof obligations, making the internal reasoning process accessible to verification and learning; (2) Logical Structured Policy Optimization learns from verifier feedback through complementary global and local rewards, jointly optimizing the overall reasoning outcome while providing targeted optimization signals to different intermediate reasoning paths; and (3) Verifier-Guided Iterative Refinement acts on verifier feedback by leveraging proof states and error messages to iteratively diagnose and repair failed reasoning. Experiments on six logical reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over strong baselines, with average improvements of 6.39% and 5.00% on Qwen3 and Llama-3.1. These results highlight the value of making logical reasoning traces verifiable, learnable, and refinable beyond final-answer supervision.
